$comment: UX-P192 — production evidence for `/weather`'s missing `<1%` / `>99%` band.
Measured 2026-08-30 against api.bainluck.com. Two separate measurements, and
they are kept apart on purpose because they answer different questions:
`population`  one atomic db-query over every outcome the weather route is
eligible to serve. Atomic because a first pass, taken as two
queries thirty minutes apart, returned 281 and 288 for the
same count — polling moves these prices every two minutes, so
a census assembled from separate queries is not a census.
`served`      a scan of the six payloads a reader's page is actually built
from. This is the number that describes the page.
THE FINDING THAT MAKES THE SHIP UNAMBIGUOUS: `exact_zero` and `unpriced` are
BOTH ZERO across the whole open weather population. There is no such thing as
an honest `0%` on this page. Every one of the 130 served zeros is printed over
a price a market is actively making, and `0%` does not read as 'unlikely' — it
`specimens` are two real markets, pulled whole, so the band can be asserted
against measured prices rather than against invented ones.
$population_comment: One query, one snapshot. Population = the outcomes of open weather markets
with a future (or absent) resolution date, updated inside seven days — i.e.
`_open_weather_query`'s own filter, so the count is over exactly the rows the
`0.995 <= p < 1`: strictly uncertain, and it renders to 100.
$served_comment: Every value on a key named `prob` in the six payloads, counted per endpoint.
`hundreds` is 0 on the day of measurement and the upper band is therefore
unexercised on the served page — but 21 rows in the population sit in it and
the featured rail rotates, so both arms ship. Saying which arm was measured
and which was reasoned about is the point of splitting this out.
$specimens_comment: Two temperature markets pulled whole from the database, both of them on the
served `/api/weather/cities` payload on the day of measurement. Every bucket
is listed, not just the offending ones, so a test can assert that the
UNCHANGED buckets really are unchanged — a band that moved a 43.5% bucket
would be a different bug wearing this one's fix.

specimens.name: Highest temperature in Los Angeles on September 1?
Highest temperature in Beijing on September 1?

$price_grid_comment: The whole distribution of the offending prices, so the band's lower arm is
sized against real quotes rather than against a hypothetical 0.0004. Note
there is nothing between 0.0045 and 0.995: the two arms are genuinely
separate populations and neither is a rounding artefact of the other.
Counted in the same window as `population` but by a SECOND query, so it may
sum to a slightly different total — prices move every two minutes. It is here
for shape, not for arithmetic, and no test adds it up.
